title: Rights and Responsibilities
bigQuestion: What rights should every person have, and what do we owe each other in return?

story.title: The Last Right on the List
story.kicker: A fourth-grade class writes its own list of rights, and the last one starts a big argument.
paragraphs: Ms. Reyes gave her class a big sheet of paper. "Today you will write a list of rights for our room," she said. "A right is something every person here should have." The class got busy right away.
The first ideas came fast. "The right to be safe." "The right to share ideas." "The right to be treated fairly." Everyone agreed. Jamal wrote each one in big letters with a green marker.
Then Lucia raised her hand. "The right to sit wherever we want!" Half the class cheered. The other half groaned. "Then my friends and I would talk all day," said Theo. "Nobody could hear the lesson."
Ms. Reyes held up her hand. "This is a real question," she said. "Grown-ups argue about it too. When does one person's right bump into someone else's? Let's think about it together."
story.think: Should the class add the right to sit anywhere? How could they make it fair for everyone?

lessons.title: Speaking and Believing Freely
lessons.mainIdea: Freedom of speech and freedom of religion let people share ideas and practice their faith.
reading: A woman writes a letter to her town newspaper. She says the town should build a new park. The mayor does not agree. But the woman is not punished. In the United States, she has *freedom of speech*.

A *right* is something every person should be free to have or do. Freedom of speech is the right to say and write your ideas. It includes ideas that leaders do not like. It does not allow lies that hurt someone or threats.

*Freedom of religion* is the right to follow any faith, or none. A family can go to a church, a mosque, a temple or a synagogue. The U.S. government may not choose one religion for everyone. Both rights are in the First Amendment.

words.d: something every person should be free to have or do
the right to say and write your ideas
the right to follow any faith, or none

look.title: The First Amendment

look.prompt: Find the words about religion and the words about speech. What does this say Congress cannot do?

check.q: What is freedom of speech?
choices: The right to follow any faith
The right to a fair trial
The right to say and write your ideas

check.q: Which part of the U.S. Constitution protects freedom of speech and religion?
check.why: The reading says both rights are in the First Amendment.

check.q: What does freedom of speech NOT allow, according to the reading?
choices: Threats and lies that hurt someone
check.why: The reading says it does not allow lies that hurt someone or threats.

lessons.title: A Fair Trial
lessons.mainIdea: A fair trial means a person accused of a crime gets a fair chance to be heard before a judge or jury.
reading: A man is accused of taking a bike. Did he really do it? He cannot just be sent to jail. First, he gets a *trial*. A trial is a meeting in a court where people decide if someone broke a law.

In a fair trial, the accused person can have a lawyer to help. The person is treated as innocent until proven guilty. Both sides tell their story. Witnesses say what they saw. Then a judge or a jury decides.

A *jury* is a group of ordinary citizens, often twelve, who listen and decide. The U.S. Sixth Amendment promises a speedy and public trial by a fair jury. Many other countries also promise fair trials, in their own ways.

words.d: a meeting in a court to decide if someone broke a law
a group of ordinary citizens who listen at a trial and decide

look.title: Is This Fair?
look.text: A girl is blamed for breaking a window at recess. The principal hears only from the boy who blamed her. The girl is not allowed to explain. Nobody asks the other kids who were there.
look.prompt: What is missing from a fair hearing here? List two things that would make it fairer.

check.q: What is a jury?
choices: A group of ordinary citizens who listen and decide
check.why: The reading defines a jury as a group of ordinary citizens who listen and decide.

check.q: In a fair trial, how is the accused person treated at first?
check.why: The reading says the person is treated as innocent until proven guilty.

check.q: Which amendment promises a speedy and public trial?
check.why: The reading names the Sixth Amendment as the promise of a speedy, public trial.

lessons.title: The Right to Vote
lessons.mainIdea: Voting is a right that has slowly grown to include more and more people.
reading: In 1920, many American women voted for president for the first time. The Nineteenth Amendment had just said women could not be denied the vote. Women had worked for this right for more than 70 years.

Voting is one of the most important rights in a democracy. The group of people who can vote is called the *electorate*. Over time, many countries made their electorate bigger. People who were left out worked hard to be included.
Today, most countries let citizens vote at age 18. The U.S. lowered its voting age from 21 to 18 in 1971. A few countries, like Austria, let people vote at 16. Countries still differ in who can vote.

words.d: all the people who are allowed to vote
a change or addition to a constitution

look.title: When Women Won the Vote
look.prompt: Which country was first? How many years later did the United States follow?

check.q: What did the Nineteenth Amendment do?
choices: Said women could not be denied the vote
check.why: The reading says the Nineteenth Amendment said women could not be denied the vote.

check.q: What is an electorate?

check.why: The chart shows New Zealand in 1893, the earliest year listed.

lessons.title: Following the Law
lessons.mainIdea: A responsibility is a duty; obeying laws is a duty that keeps everyone safe.
reading: A driver comes to a red light late at night. No other cars are around. Should she stop? Yes. The law says so. Following laws even when no one is watching helps everyone trust each other.
A *responsibility* is something you are expected to do. Rights and responsibilities go together. You have the right to be safe. You also have the responsibility not to put others in danger.

What if a law seems unfair? In a democracy, people can work to change it. They can write letters, speak at meetings and vote. Some people choose *civil disobedience*, which means breaking an unfair law peacefully and accepting the punishment.

words.d: something you are expected to do; a duty
breaking a law you think is unfair, peacefully, and accepting the punishment

look.title: Right and Responsibility Pairs
look.text: Right: to be safe at school. Responsibility: to keep hands to yourself. Right: to share your ideas. Responsibility: to let others share theirs. Right: to use the library. Responsibility: ?
look.prompt: What responsibility would you pair with the right to use the library? Make one more pair of your own.

check.q: What is a responsibility?
choices: Something you are expected to do
check.why: The reading says a responsibility is something you are expected to do.

check.q: What can people in a democracy do about a law that seems unfair?
choices: Work to change it by writing, speaking and voting
check.why: The reading lists writing letters, speaking at meetings and voting.

check.q: What is civil disobedience?
choices: Breaking an unfair law peacefully and accepting the punishment
check.why: The reading defines civil disobedience this way.

lessons.title: Serving on a Jury
lessons.mainIdea: Jury duty is a responsibility that makes the right to a fair trial possible.
reading: One day a letter comes to Maya's house. It is for her dad. It says he has been called for *jury duty*. He must go to the county courthouse. He may help decide a real case.
Remember the right to a fair trial? It needs a jury of ordinary people. That only works if citizens show up. So serving on a jury is a responsibility. Adult citizens can be called to serve.

Jurors must listen carefully to both sides. They must decide only on the facts shown in court. They must keep an open mind. Some people find it a hassle. Many others say it helped them understand how courts work.

words.d: the responsibility of citizens to serve on a jury when called
one member of a jury

look.title: A Good Juror
look.text: Juror 1 decided before the trial began. Juror 2 listened to every witness and took notes. Juror 3 looked up the case on a phone at home, which the judge said not to do.
look.prompt: Which juror did the job well? What did the other two do wrong?

check.q: Why is jury duty a responsibility?
choices: It makes money for the town
Fair trials need ordinary citizens to serve
check.why: The reading says a fair trial needs a jury, so citizens must show up.

check.q: What must jurors decide on?
choices: Only the facts shown in court
check.why: The reading says jurors must decide only on the facts shown in court.

check.q: What is a juror?
check.why: A juror is one member of a jury.

lessons.title: Paying Taxes and Voting
lessons.mainIdea: Paying taxes and voting are ways citizens help run their community.
reading: The new playground at the park did not appear by magic. Tax money paid for the swings and slides. When adults pay taxes, they help pay for things everyone shares. Paying taxes is a responsibility.

Voting is both a right and a responsibility. When people vote, they help choose leaders and decide questions. When few people vote, a small group makes choices for everyone. Being an *informed voter* means learning about the choices first.
Countries handle this in different ways. In the U.S., voting is a choice. In Australia, voting is required by law. Adults who skip it may pay a small fine. People disagree about which way is better.

words.d: a voter who learns about the choices before voting
money people and businesses pay to the government

look.title: Two Ways to Vote
look.text: Country A: Voting is a choice. Adults can vote or stay home. Country B: Voting is required. Adults who do not vote may pay a small fine. Supporters of B say more voices get heard. Supporters of A say freedom includes the choice not to vote.
look.prompt: Give one reason for each country's rule. Which reason do you find stronger, and why?

check.q: What paid for the new playground in the reading?
check.why: The reading says tax money paid for the swings and slides.

check.q: What is an informed voter?
choices: A voter who learns about the choices first
check.why: The reading defines an informed voter this way.

check.q: In which country is voting required by law?
check.why: The reading says in Australia voting is required by law.

lessons.title: A Promise for the World
lessons.mainIdea: In 1948, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, led by Eleanor Roosevelt.
reading: World War II ended in 1945. Millions of people had died. Many had been treated horribly. Leaders from many countries said, "Never again." They wanted a list of rights for every person on Earth.

Eleanor Roosevelt led the group that wrote it. She had been First Lady of the United States. People from China, Lebanon, France, Chile and other places helped. On December 10, 1948, the United Nations adopted the *Universal Declaration of Human Rights*.

It lists 30 articles of *human rights*. These are rights every person has just by being human. They include the right to life, to fair trials and to free speech. The declaration is a promise, not a law every country must obey.

words.d: rights every person has just by being human
a list of rights for all people, adopted by the United Nations in 1948

look.title: Article 1
look.text: "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood."
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 1, 1948
look.prompt: Put Article 1 in your own words. Which part is about rights, and which part is about how we should act?

check.q: Who led the group that wrote the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
check.why: The reading says Eleanor Roosevelt led the writing group.

check.q: When did the United Nations adopt the declaration?
check.why: The reading gives the date as December 10, 1948.

check.q: What are human rights?
choices: Rights only for citizens of one country
Rights only for adults who vote
Rights every person has just by being human
check.why: The reading defines human rights as rights every person has by being human.

lessons.title: Different Countries, Different Ways
lessons.mainIdea: Countries protect rights in different ways, through constitutions, laws and courts.
reading: In the United States, many rights are written in the *Bill of Rights*. These are the first ten amendments to the Constitution, added in 1791. Courts use them to decide if a law is fair.

Other countries do it differently. The United Kingdom has no single written constitution. Its rights come from many laws and old court rulings. Germany's Basic Law of 1949 begins by saying human dignity must be protected.

India's constitution lists Fundamental Rights, like equality before the law. Some countries write rights down but do not protect them in real life. So people ask two questions. Are rights written down? Are they really kept?

words.d: the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, which list basic rights
the worth and respect every person deserves

look.title: Written or Kept?
look.text: Country A has a long list of rights in its constitution, but reporters who criticize leaders are jailed. Country B has no single written constitution, but courts protect people who criticize leaders.
look.prompt: In which country is free speech safer in real life? What does this tell you about writing rights down?

check.q: What is the Bill of Rights?
choices: The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution
check.why: The reading says the Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, added in 1791.

check.q: Which country has no single written constitution?
check.why: The reading says the UK's rights come from many laws and court rulings.

check.q: What two questions does the reading say people ask about rights?
choices: Who is king? Who is queen?
How old is it? Who wrote it?
Are rights written down? Are they really kept?
Is it long? Is it short?
check.why: The reading ends with those two questions.

lessons.title: Disagreeing With Respect
lessons.mainIdea: In a free country, people disagree often, and they can do it with respect.
reading: Remember Lucia and Theo? Lucia wanted the right to sit anywhere. Theo worried the room would be too noisy. They both had good reasons. Neither one was a bad person for thinking differently.

When people have rights like free speech, they will disagree. That is normal. *Respectful disagreement* means sharing your view while treating the other person kindly. You listen, you ask questions and you attack ideas, not people.
Sometimes people find a *compromise*. Each side gives up a little to reach a deal. Ms. Reyes's class might agree: sit anywhere on Fridays, if the room stays quiet enough to learn.

words.d: sharing a different view while treating the other person kindly
a deal where each side gives up a little

look.title: Which Reply Is Respectful?
look.text: Theo says, "Free seating will be too loud." Reply A: "That's a dumb idea, Theo." Reply B: "I see why you worry. What if we tried it one day a week?" Reply C: Lucia rolls her eyes and turns away.
look.prompt: Which reply shows respectful disagreement? Rewrite one of the other replies to make it respectful.

check.q: What is a compromise?
choices: A deal where each side gives up a little
check.why: The reading defines a compromise as each side giving up a little.

check.q: In respectful disagreement, what do you attack?
check.why: The reading says you attack ideas, not people.

check.q: What compromise does the reading suggest for Ms. Reyes's class?
choices: Sit anywhere on Fridays if the room stays quiet enough
check.why: The reading suggests sitting anywhere on Fridays if the room stays quiet.

lessons.title: Gandhi and King
lessons.mainIdea: Gandhi in India and Martin Luther King Jr. in the U.S. used peaceful protest to win rights.
reading: In 1930, Mohandas Gandhi began a long walk to the sea in India. Britain ruled India then and taxed salt. Gandhi walked about 240 miles. At the sea, he made his own salt. Thousands joined him. This was the Salt March.
Gandhi believed in *nonviolent protest*, which means standing up for change without hurting anyone. His work helped India win independence in 1947. Leaders in other countries studied his ideas.

Martin Luther King Jr. was one of them. He led the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955 and 1956. In 1963, he spoke at the March on Washington. He worked peacefully to end *segregation*, the unfair separation of Black and white Americans.

words.d: standing up for change without hurting anyone
keeping people apart by race, by law or by custom

look.title: King's Dream
look.text: King said he dreamed that one day his four little children would live in a nation where they would be judged by who they are inside, not by the color of their skin.
look.cite: Martin Luther King Jr., speech at the March on Washington, 1963
look.prompt: What did King hope for his children? How does this connect to Article 1 of the Universal Declaration?

check.q: Why did Gandhi make his own salt?
choices: To protest Britain's tax on salt
check.why: The reading says Britain taxed salt, and Gandhi made salt to protest.

check.q: What is nonviolent protest?
choices: Standing up for change without hurting anyone
check.why: The reading defines nonviolent protest this way.

check.q: What did King work to end?
check.why: The reading says King worked peacefully to end segregation.

lessons.title: Nelson Mandela
lessons.mainIdea: Nelson Mandela helped end apartheid and became South Africa's first president elected by all races.
reading: For many years, South Africa had a system called *apartheid*. The word means apartness. Laws kept people apart by race. Black South Africans could not vote in national elections. They were forced into separate schools and neighborhoods.

Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid. He was sent to prison and stayed there for 27 years. People around the world called for his release. He was freed in 1990. He then worked with leaders who had once been his enemies.

In 1994, South Africans of all races voted together for the first time. Mandela was elected president. He chose *reconciliation*, bringing people back together, instead of revenge. He wanted one South Africa for everyone.

words.d: the system of laws in South Africa that kept people apart by race
bringing people back together after a conflict

look.title: Mandela's Road
look.prompt: How many years passed between Mandela's release and his election? What happened in between?

check.q: What does the word apartheid mean?
check.why: The reading says apartheid means apartness.

check.q: How long was Mandela in prison?
check.why: The reading says he stayed in prison for 27 years.

check.q: What did Mandela choose instead of revenge?
check.why: The reading says he chose reconciliation, bringing people together.

review.q: How are Gandhi, King and Mandela alike?

review.q: What is the best way to disagree respectfully?

review.q: Why might a country with rights written down still not protect them?

review.why: The chapter says people ask both whether rights are written and whether they are really kept.
